item.title: Links 9/3/2026
This Labor Day: forecast, backcast, rest, and dream
item.description:
How have the ways you labor changed over the years? My very first job that my social security benefits will register goes back to working in a local Roy Rogers fast food restaurant at age 16, serving fried chicken and biscuits. I was on my feet most of the day and took pride in inserting my time card into the punch clock machine registering the start of my shift with that satisfying hole puncher crunch sound. Over the years my labor has varied, from jobs requiring me to be able-bodied (working catering jobs as a food server long into the night); to the humility required for anonymous temp jobs until something better came along; to a hybrid version of physical movement and mental activity (when I was a middle school English teacher); to work that leveraged my intellectual capacity and knowledge — as a professor and now as a creativity strategist. 

That diversity of labor has been a privilege.

Thank goodness that by the 1880’s, efforts from the carpenter and machinist unions led to the ratification of Labor Day as a national holiday in the United States. Depending on my life stage, my emotional state over Labor Day weekend has been a total spectrum ranging from full relaxation to anxiety and nostalgia. I can remember Labor Day signaling the last lazy days of summer as a child and the excitement I felt about entering a new grade of school. I can also recall those years as a professor when Labor Day made me feel a bit anxious as I made finishing touches on a syllabus for a brand new course, uncertain if the learning experience would be a hit or bomb with the students. 

As the U.S labor movement grew, and laborers organized, the recognition that rest was essential for us to produce our best work became as predominant as fair pay and wages. When I researched the content for Move. Think. Rest., a book that explores an alternative, human-centered way for us to think about productivity called the MTR (pronounced motor) system, the prevailing insight I had is that our best work must be cultivated, not simply produced. When we cultivate our work we not only focus on efficiencies, output and metrics, but we also incorporate the time needed to let ideas marinate, to collaborate fully, and to value slow as much as fast.

As I think about this upcoming Labor Day weekend, I invite you to indulge in some backcasting and forecasting. Whether you manage a team, have just started a new job, or feel like you’re slogging your way through the motions, I encourage you to use this Labor Day weekend to hit pause. Here are three prompts that I used in a recent microretreat I designed for myself. Choose one or all of them — but do allow yourself to slow down and consider how these prompts can help you to cultivate your best work. Don’t spend more than 20 minutes on each prompt.

Promp #1:  The 25 Year Time Horizon. Pick a moment in time 20 years ago, and describe your personal condition from a physical, social, emotional, and spiritual perspective. Then, pick a different moment in time that occurred just five years ago, and again delineate where you were from a physical, social, emotional, and spiritual perspective. When I did this exercise, the 20-year backcast was a time when I was in a pretty vulnerable state. I had gone through a really bad breakup, and I wasn’t happy with my job. On the other hand, I was thrilled to be traveling the globe and experiencing different cultures. Then the point I focused on, that happened just five years ago, was shortly after turning 50 years old. I was married, a homeowner, an entrepreneur and had a very clear sense of myself. When we do this backcasting exercise it grounds us and gives us perspective on any worries and concerns we may presently have. 

Prompt #2: Big Breaks. Sometimes I call this the “It Just Takes One” exercise. List 10 big breaks in your life that have happened in the personal and professional dimensions. This backcasting exercise is really cool because it goes into a category of acknowledging that exponential change often happens from small moments.  It only takes that one introduction, that one encounter, that one email, that one break to open the aperture of opportunity. There’s something about acknowledging the people and circumstances, and times when we decide to show up, that really builds momentum and traction. What’s cool about the big breaks exercise is that you can go into the office on the Tuesday after Labor Day weekend and do this exercise with your team. Thinking about big breaks within the organization can build momentum for the fourth quarter of the year.

Prompt #3: The Dream State. This forecasting exercise helps us to get really audacious and blue sky in our thinking. The question I pose is “Where would I love to be in five years? Who do I desire to be in 5 years?  What would it take for me to get there?” What emerges may surprise you. Notice that I used verbs like love and desire — not like or need. And if you already did the 20 Year vs. Five Year Arc exercise, then you’re astutely aware of what’s feasible in a five year time horizon. Just consider how much the world changed between January 2020 and January 2025!

These are very heart-centered, emotional exercises that fuel how we labor. They’re not solely mental exercises about what’s practical or feasible in our current state. These prompts are designed to liberate you. 

So spend your Labor Day weekend doing some backcasting and some forecasting. Rest and dream in honor of the laborers who came before us, and out of respect for the seeds you’ve sown over the years.

item.title: New report: El Niño 2026 is now the strongest in 1,000 years. Here’s what that means for your winter forecast
item.description:
El Niño is now the strongest it has been in 1,000 years, according to new research from the University of Michigan, which reconstructed ocean surface temperatures over the last millennium by looking at fossilized corals in the Galápagos Islands.

The study, published in the journal Science, found a large recent increase in the variability of sea surface temperature in the eastern equatorial Pacific compared to previous existing paleorecords. That increase also parallels rising global temperature and results from stronger El Niño events.

“We’ve been seeing some very strong El Niño events in the late 20th and early 21st century, and what we didn’t know was how unusual those are,” said lead study author Julie Cole, environmental scientist at the University of Michigan.

“We found that, on average, El Niño events have been stronger in the past 40 years than at any time in the past millennium, with higher temperatures that lead to more powerful effects on weather,” Cole wrote in the Conversation.

She explained temperatures across the equatorial Pacific Ocean have warmed dramatically in 2026, signaling the onset of a strong and potentially historic El Niño—which could affect weather not just in the Pacific, but across the U.S. and around the world—as El Niño events become stronger and more destructive.

The results provide a long-term framework for understanding the Pacific El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and how it is impacting ecosystems, infrastructure, and humans worldwide, the study said.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Climate Prediction Center is also saying El Niño is strengthening, with a greater than 90% chance of a “very strong event” in the Northern Hemisphere during the 2026 hurricane season this fall or winter.

What is El Niño?

El Niño is a complex weather pattern, referring to the warming of the ocean surface, or above-average sea surface temperatures, in the Pacific Ocean.

Winds that normally blow from west to east weaken—and in some cases, they blow east—disrupting normal weather and creating more extreme meteorological events, per the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS). As the winds “take warm water from South America towards Asia,” that’s replaced by cold water that rises, known as “upwelling,” according to NOAA.

The results: intensifying storms and flooding here in the U.S., particularly in the Southeast and Gulf Coast, which can also create wildfires and drought. The 2015 Super El Niño caused a significant Caribbean drought.

item.title: This EPA proposal on data centers could leave the public in the dark about air pollution
item.description:
A plan by the Environmental Protection Agency could make it harder for the public to learn about and comment on proposed AI data centers that have sparked backlash in communities across the United States and transformed the midterm election landscape.

The EPA proposal would eliminate a federal requirement that states notify the public and seek comment before issuing air pollution permits for data centers and other industrial facilities. States could still offer opportunities for public comment, but the EPA would no longer mandate them as a condition for states to grant permits.

Critics say the move could thwart local residents from learning about proposed data centers or making their voices heard before projects are approved and construction begins. The move comes during a widespread backlash as tech giants build hundreds of massive server warehouses to fuel artificial intelligence and cloud computing.

“By eliminating the long-standing federal requirement for public notice, this proposal continues efforts by the Trump administration to turn its back on the fundamental EPA principle of transparency,” said Mike Koerber, a former deputy director of EPA’s air quality office.

If made final, the plan could create “an unlevel playing field where citizens in one state are kept completely in the dark about new data centers and heavy industrial emissions in their backyards, while neighboring states maintain oversight,” he said.
Under the EPA plan, states with weak or no requirements for public comment could speed permits for data centers, power plants and other pollution sources without consulting the public or even informing communities where the facilities are located, Koerber and other critics said.

Communities deserve a chance to weigh in, advocates say

“Data centers and other industrial sources should not be able to get their air pollution permits in secret,” said Keri Powell, senior attorney for the Southern Environmental Law Center, an advocacy organization that leads a coalition of nearly 200 environmental, health and community groups that filed comments with the EPA opposing the plan. “Communities deserve a chance to weigh in” before potentially harmful projects are approved.

An EPA spokesperson called that a false narrative.

“In our proposal we are saying that states get to pick how they want their permitting process to go for minor sources” of air pollution, spokesperson Carolyn Holran said.

The EPA proposal does not specifically identify data centers, she said, noting that the plan also would apply to laundromats, car repair shops and even landfills and steel mills that are considered “minor” pollution sources under the federal Clean Air Act.

The proposal does not demand that states make particular changes to their programs, nor does it alter federal emission standards or weaken environmental protections, Holran said. “Rather, the proposal simply aligns the national program with the Clean Air Act language to ensure that states are in the lead regarding their programs.”

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, who has made U.S. leadership in AI a top agency priority, said in a statement that the plan is aimed at “cutting unnecessary and burdensome red tape, unleashing American energy and advancing cooperative federalism” with states. The EPA is expected to make the rule final next year.
President Donald Trump continues to stick up for data centers, even as politicians from both parties criticize them and many communities try to block them. Trump said on social media this week that U.S. communities that don’t have data centers will “end up being backwards and poor.”

Trump says data centers are crucial in the AI race against China

Trump has acknowledged that data centers need “a little public relations help” and has pushed tech companies to generate their own electricity to shield consumers from higher utility bills. The Republican president calls data centers critical to winning the AI race against China.

Environmental groups and other critics say the EPA proposal ignores the reality that many states, particularly in the South and Midwest, don’t require public notice or hearings beyond those set by federal agencies. The federal plan would leave many communities in the dark before data centers show up in their backyards, they said.
“It’s beyond cruel for Trump’s EPA to silence front-line communities who bear the brunt of unhealthy air,” said Brandon Jones-Cobb, a senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity, another environmental group.

The EPA “has already turned its back on science, cut enforcement against industrial polluters and eliminated life-saving air pollution measures,” he said. “Now it wants to shut the public out of decisions to build or expand facilities that expose communities to dangerous air pollution, including data centers.”

Powell, whose organization focuses on six Southern states from Virginia to Alabama, said many states “only do what is required by federal law” when it comes to public notice of land-use projects and other environmental concerns.

“We rely on a minimum federal requirement to ensure we have environmental protections and a voice,” she said in an interview, calling regulation of data centers a crucial issue in a region where the energy-hungry behemoths are proliferating. Virginia and Georgia are both among states with the highest concentration of current and proposed data centers.

Americans worry data centers could cause pollution, job losses

Besides powering AI and cloud computing, data centers are often sources of nitrogen oxide, which helps form ozone, as well as carbon monoxide and other air pollutants. Local communities also have expressed concerns about excessive water use and noise from data centers. Many Americans worry that AI could increase economic disparities and cause widespread job losses.

Data center advocates stress that local taxes paid by the centers can help fund public schools, reducing the financial burden on homeowners.

Jane Williams, executive director of California Communities Against Toxics, said even if data centers ultimately are approved, “every community should be able to participate robustly in governmental decisions that can pollute our air.”

Rolling back the EPA rule “pulls a dark cloud, filled with soot and toxic chemicals, over communities’ right to know what polluting facilities are planned in their community,” she said.

—Matthew Daly, Associated Press

item.title: Trump loves data centers, voters don’t. Of course he’s doubling down right before the midterms.
item.description:
Americans don’t agree about much in 2026, but a majority are in lockstep on data centers. According to recent polling, a full 75% oppose having one built anywhere near them, a number within striking distance of the 84% of Americans who oppose cutting Social Security. 

Because the U.S. economy is now profoundly dependent on artificial intelligence, the growing unpopularity of the data centers that supply it is a big problem. Never fear, however, because Donald Trump and his cronies in Congress and media have a bold new strategy for solving it. They’ve lately started claiming data centers are unpopular only with backwards fools and those who’ve been deviously duped by an elaborate Chinese propaganda operation.

It’s a messaging tactic that seems destined to be received as poorly as, well, data centers themselves. With midterm elections two months away, the timing could hardly be worse.  

How data centers became toxic

As recently as January 2025, data centers were considered a widely palatable necessity of our glorious AI future. Those who were against AI altogether were obviously also against data centers, but everyone else generally had less of a fixed opinion. 

One of Joe Biden’s final acts as president was an executive order to accelerate AI data-center development, something his administration framed as essential for “national security, economic competitiveness, AI safety and clean energy growth.” In a photo-negative image of where the public stands now, data centers in January 2025 were among the only things Biden and Trump agreed on. One of the latter’s first moves after returning to power was announcing Stargate, a $500 billion investment in data centers and AI infrastructure in the U.S.

By the end of 2025, though, public sentiment had soured far beyond never-AI absolutists. While proponents touted the nearly 5,000 U.S. data centers as job creators that boost local economies, complaints about them were tangible, easy to understand and, crucially, bipartisan. These structures took up too much land, consumed too much water, drove up utility bills, and disrupted rural life with their thunderous noise and air pollution. Not to mention the lucrative tax breaks for tech overlords, and reduced public funds for local services. 

Anti-data center animosity could no longer be waved away as a byproduct of Woke. Not when Trump voters in Pennsylvania were part of the pushback. 

Throughout 2026, the shift away from data centers has rapidly spiked. The Annenberg Public Policy Center found that opposition to having them built in one’s community shot up 12 points between spring and summer, from 49% to 61%. All signs pointed to data centers becoming a liability during the midterms for any politician who favors them.

It should surprise no one that the Democratic politicians Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have been calling for a moratorium on new data centers, or that, in July, New York became the first state to implement one. However, when Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican, in August announced a moratorium on data centers in Texas, the sea change became impossible to ignore. 

Backlash to the backlash

Internal polling on data centers among Republicans is now apocalyptic, according to an Axios report on August 19, which compared the facilities’ popularity to that of “spent nuclear waste.” It was in this inhospitable environment that Trump apparently decided to push back on the pushback.

Up until quite recently, Trump had simply defended data centers, calling them “beautiful” last month. This week, he pivoted to an offensive blitz, attacking those opposed to them. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers,” he wrote on TruthSocial on Monday, “is if they want to end up being backwards and poor.” 

The president ended his missive by noting, “China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement,” further shaming his fans who dared to form a different opinion. Soon enough, his flunkies in Congress and conservative media seized on that aspect of his messaging strategy and took it to new conspiratorial heights. 

On Tuesday morning, Steve Scalise, the House majority leader, announced during an interview with Fox Business that an investigation is supposedly underway to determine whether the fervor against data centers perhaps stems from a China-driven misinformation campaign. 

What other possible explanation could there be?

Shortly afterward, Brian Kilmeade, the Fox & Friends cohost, picked up the thread, claiming that a lot of the American hostility toward data centers is due to “bad information,” which was “put out by our competitors slash enemies,” meaning China, along with “other social media groups that look to influence our elections,” he claimed, by “using bots and . . . maybe influencers to start turning the American public against data centers.” Whew!

Kilmeade seems to have forgotten the hard lesson Fox News learned back in May. That’s when Shark Tank’s resident heel, Kevin O’Leary, made a similar statement on the network, claiming the nonprofit group opposing his planned massive data center in Utah was “funded by China or the Chinese Communist Party.” This gambit apparently did not go unnoticed by the legal representatives of the nonprofit Alliance for a Better Utah. 

O’Leary ended up walking back his unsubstantiated claim and admitting he had no evidence to support it, while Fox News apologized for airing it. Perhaps because Kilmeade named no specific entity being bribed by China into astroturfing anti-data center invective, he won’t be forced to make a similar retraction.

In any case, the recent full-court press admonishing U.S. citizens for having the wrong opinion about data centers has left the president and his defenders open to counterattacks. 

Reporters are already hounding elected Republicans about whether they agree with Trump’s “backwards and poor” comment. Politicians like Ocasio-Cortez and Justin Pearson, a Democratic state representative in Tennessee, wondered aloud, in separate press conferences this week, why Trump doesn’t install a data center close to Mar-a-Lago if they are as wonderful as he says.

The same old cognitive dissonance

Trump’s insistence that data centers are good, actually, despite all the documented reasons to the contrary, should feel familiar by now. For the past decade, he has consistently portrayed himself as the sole arbiter of truth in a dishonest world. 

Lately, though, the staggering falsity of his more outlandish claims may be getting harder to swallow for all but his most fervent fans.   

If Iran is “completely defeated,” why are we still at war—and why is gas so expensive?

If vandals are responsible for damaging Trump’s Reflecting Pool renovation, why have charges against all of them been dismissed?

And if the 2020 election was rigged, which he insisted again most recently with a televised speech back in July, why has no supporting evidence whatsoever emerged yet?

There’s no polling as of this writing about how Trump’s most recent messaging on data centers has gone over, but even 35% of Republicans in an Economist/YouGov poll disagreed with his statement in August about embracing them.

As we careen toward the midterms, Trump’s sweaty claims about the supposed beauty of data centers just may broadly come across as authentic as one of his AI slop posts on Truth Social.

item.title: The largest school system in the U.S. just banned AI for students through 8th grade
item.description:
New York City’s public schools will temporarily ban elementary and middle school students from using generative artificial intelligence tools during the upcoming school year, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Wednesday.

The one-year moratorium — part of a broader assessment of how children in the nation’s largest school system interact with the technology — will apply to “all software that uses student-facing generative AI” for students through eighth grade, the mayor’s office said. It described the policy as the most expansive prohibition in the country.

At the same time, the city will establish twice-yearly AI literacy classes for all public high school students. It will also launch pilot programs allowing some high school students to use a handful of AI platforms under an educator’s supervision. Companion chatbots will be prohibited across all grades, officials said.

The approach comes as students, parents and schools across the country attempt to navigate the use of AI tools in the classroom and elsewhere. Schools are working to teach children how to incorporate the technology while preventing them from relying too heavily on it or using it to cheat.

“Each day when our children come to school, we teach them to ask questions, to challenge assumptions, to interrogate the premise, to ask why. When it comes to AI in our schools, we hold an obligation to do the same,” Mamdani, a Democrat, said at a news conference.

The Los Angeles school district, where students returned to classrooms in mid-August, is temporarily blocking access to generative AI tools on student devices across all grades.

The Los Angeles Unified School District said Wednesday that the ban will remain in place across the country’s second-largest school district as officials develop a student AI policy during the school year.

In June, LAUSD became the first major school district to eliminate the use of school-issued devices for its youngest students as part of a sweeping screen time policy. The policy banned devices before second grade, set screen time limits for all grades and blocked YouTube and other social media sites during the school day.
In New York, the city will also recommend screen time limits for students, suggesting a daily cap of 30 minutes for students in grades three through five and 45 minutes for those in grades six through eight. Teachers will be allowed to use AI for instructional planning and operational tasks.

At least 37 states have official AI guidance that schools can use as a blueprint, though there is no single definition of AI literacy or consensus on how it should be taught. New York state last year approved a ban on students’ use of cellphones in schools.

City education officials will also conduct a broad review of all technology tools used in the school system and eliminate those deemed nonessential to learning.

Michael Mulgrew, president of the United Federation of Teachers in New York, praised the screen time limits but said the city’s AI policy “leaves many questions unanswered,” including how the Education Department “will be more aggressive in demanding the products it purchases have AI safeguards.”

Josh Golin, executive director of the children’s advocacy group Fairplay, said he would have preferred a longer moratorium and more time between the announcement and the start of the school year.

“A year to evaluate is not nearly enough time,” he said, adding that the onus should be on AI platforms “to demonstrate that their products are effective at teaching kids, that they’re safe, that they’re not displacing face-to-face interaction and that they’re not leading to rampant cheating.”

New York City public school students are scheduled to return to classrooms next week.

Associated Press writer Jocelyn Gecker contributed to this report.

—Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press

item.title: The AI doctor will see you soon. We don’t have a plan for that
item.description:
In the movie Elysium, set in the year 2154, Matt Damon plays Max Da Costa, a criminal lowlife trying his damndest to leave Earth. Up above, the wealthy elite live on a ring-shaped space station, where disease and poverty have been eradicated. Most of the population, however, still lives on Earth, and they are struggling to survive each day. They can only dream of ever making it to the space station in the sky. But for Max, getting to Elysium is a matter of survival: He needs access to healthcare that can save his own life.

Even in the imaginary world of Elysium, 125 years into the future, high-quality, AI-driven healthcare is only for the privileged few. The ultrawealthy, who were able to escape an impoverished and overpopulated planet, live in tranquil luxury in space. This dystopian portrayal of healthcare’s vast inequities is unfortunately more realistic than we would like to believe. But our future doesn’t have to be this stark. 

Imagine Sam, a man in his 50s who walks into his doctor’s office complaining of chest pain. First, the doctor asks Sam about his symptom history and risk factors; then doctor performs a physical assessment, taking vitals like heart rate and blood pressure. The doctor might request additional tests, such as an ECG, a blood test, or chest X-ray. All these data help the physician make a list of differential diagnoses, such as angina, heart attack, or just acid reflux. Based on training and experience, the doctor makes a diagnosis and proposes additional tests and treatment options.

Today, these functions are the domain of human expertise—doctors, nurses, and providers who undergo highly specialized education and on-the-job training. But that may not be the case for long. Within the next decade, Sam may be seeing an artificial intelligence doctor for his common healthcare needs and day-to-day management. 

The transition to medicine supported and eventually delivered by algorithms —what I call autonomous health—promises to make healthcare more convenient, accessible, and affordable. Imagine no more waiting to see a doctor. In 2025, there was an estimated shortfall of 35,600 physicians and 25,200 surgeons. We have the highest per-capita spend on healthcare in the developed world, yet annual healthcare premiums for employers are going up 6.5-7% this year.

Increasing automation is the only path to mitigate the access shortages and increasing cost challenges in healthcare. LLM researchers have demonstrated incredible ability to distill medical knowledge. Many already visit ChatGPT and Claude for healthcare answers before they see their doctor. 

But this also raises a flurry of questions. Foremost, can we ensure these technologies are safe and clinically validated? How do we develop a hybrid model of care, where humans and AI systems work together as a care team? What will the experience of the healthcare consumer be in this new world?

And then there are the bigger structural questions. Does the financial model of healthcare need to support a path towards increasing autonomy? What should happen to reimbursement rates for clinical visits? How will this impact today’s professional workforce? Will we need even more healthcare professionals, but perhaps with different skills than today’s doctors? Would AI-enabled care be reserved, Elysium-like, for the privileged few? Or might we see the inverse, where automation is common among the masses at lower costs, while healthcare with human expertise comes at a premium?

We can’t even begin to answer these questions until we have a frame of reference, some sense of where we’re going and where we want to be. 

Consider the self-driving car. For years, manufacturers used terms like “autonomous,” “automated,” and “self-driving” in their press and marketing, interchangeably and without clear distinctions. This led to widespread confusion about the capabilities and limitations of competing automated driving systems among consumers and regulators.

The Society of Automotive Engineers proposed a solution. They defined a standard for driving automation systems for motor vehicles, which established different levels of automation, from driver assistance aids to fully automated driving. SAE J3016, adopted in 2016, became a cornerstone in the development of autonomous driving technology. Every automaker used it to benchmark their systems, and it gave governments and regulatory bodies a clear framework to create laws, set safety standards, and ensure the safe deployment of automated vehicles. It eliminated the friction that would have held the industry back.

In many ways, AI in healthcare is where self-driving vehicles were a decade ago. Tech companies, medical start-ups, hospital systems, and even insurance companies are now caught up in their own hype cycle. To provide scientific context amid all the noise, I propose four levels for autonomy in healthcare, as part of a framework that can help regulators, administrators, and all of us evaluate and adopt new technologies: No Automation, Light Automation, High Automation, and—perhaps at some point—Complete Automation.

Level 1: No Automation

Across the planet, the average person today experiences little to no automation in their care. Whether a person walks into a concierge doctor’s office in Fort Lauderdale or a rural clinic in Namibia, the diagnosis and treatment decision, even for a simple common cold, is made by a physician. 

This is not to discount the widespread access to blood and lab testing, as well as advances in medical imaging. More than 4 billion imaging tests, such as X-rays, CT scans, and MRIs, are done every year across the world. These data are invaluable, but the interpretation and diagnosis, and the recommended treatment are still heavily dependent on human medical expertise.

Level 2: Light Automation

Light automation, or automated assistance for human doctors and medical providers, is akin to cruise control in your car. Adaptive cruise control maintains a set following distance from the vehicle ahead, and lane-keep assist gently steers the car back into its lane if it starts to drift. These features don’t replace human drivers, but they help prevent common mistakes that occur when a human driver may be distracted or fatigued, often due to the sheer monotony of driving. 

Level 2 for healthcare is happening now. But unlike adaptive cruise control, these Level 2 doctor assistance systems are not managing mundane, monotonous, mechanical tasks. Instead, they help human doctors and nurses with diagnoses, usually by summarizing or processing large swathes of additional complex data. 

Algorithms now play a role in assisting with diagnosis in imaging, such as radiology and cancer detection, and in the identification of risk factors based on genetic data and markers. Without computational analysis, for instance, it is physically impossible for a human doctor to sift through genomic data and confirm the gene expression of BRCA1 or TP53 [genes that repair DNA and prevent cancer] for a patient during a 15-minute appointment.

As of summer 2026, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had authorized more than 1500 AI or machine learning (ML) algorithms for market use. The vast majority of these, about 76%, are in radiology. Most of these make imaging refinements, such as improving image quality, but a growing number are now helping clinicians make better clinical diagnoses. These ML algorithms and models are assisting radiologists in making a better decision, not replacing them. Even now, all the AI and ML algorithms cleared by the FDA require a human to be in the loop. 

If 99% of healthcare diagnostic and treatment decisions made every day on planet Earth are at Level 1: No Automation, the remaining 1% are at Level 2: Light Automation. But the share of care being provided with light automation is growing rapidly, with hundreds of new algorithms being approved by the FDA every year.

Level 3: High Automation

From a purely algorithmic perspective, the rapidly improving ability of AI is leading us toward Level 3: High Automation. With high automation, a meaningful percentage of diagnosis and treatment decisions are entirely automated and made by algorithms. 

Today, doctors and healthcare professionals make hundreds of decisions every day. At a high level, there are diagnosis decisions, treatment decisions, and clinical interventions such as surgery. Over a year ago, MedGemini and MedPrompt, from Google and Microsoft respectively, achieved a competitive accuracy of 91.1 and 90.2, exceeding human experts (87.01) on U.S. Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE) benchmarks, a dataset of realistic medical exam questions that requires clinical knowledge and reasoning ability. In the last year, researchers have further shown AI agents, integrated with electronic health record (EHR) data, are exceeding the performance of human diagnostic decisions based on clinical data.

To understand the impact this could have on healthcare, let’s rewind. Over a decade ago, at my previous company, Ginger, a unique collaboration began to take shape. Dr. Sai Moturu, a computer scientist, joined forces with Dr. Mimi Winsburg, a leading psychiatrist, and other expert colleagues, to tackle one of psychiatry’s most complex challenges: choosing the right SSRI for a new patient’s first treatment. 

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) such as Prozac and Zoloft are antidepressants typically prescribed for anxiety, depression, and PTSD, often alongside psychotherapy or coaching. The decision to prescribe an SSRI is based on a patient’s clinical state, symptoms, lifestyle factors, other comorbid chronic conditions, related medications, and past response to an SSRI. For example, Prozac may have a higher risk of interactions with other medications the patient is taking, but it also has a longer half-life than Zoloft, making it better for patients who occasionally miss doses. A human psychiatrist evaluates the patient, considers these and other factors, and may suggest an appropriate SSRI drug to treat the patient’s symptoms.

By blending a machine learning approach with extensive clinical experience, this cross-functional team of experts built decision-tree models that incorporated clinical history and lifestyle data to match the judgment of a panel of experienced psychiatrists. The results were striking. In head-to-head evaluations across dozens of real-world cases, they found that their ML decision tree model selected the correct initial SSRI over 90% of the time. As in typical practice, dosages could be changed or medications would be updated based on a patient’s response, creating new branches in the treatment decision tree.

This is a relatively simple example of machines’ decision-making potential for treatments in behavioral health. But the potential impact on access to and costs of healthcare would be tremendous. Today, amid a shortage of providers, an estimated 55% of adults with mental health needs go without treatment. What would the economic benefit be if a quarter of cases of depression that need a psychiatrist but can’t find one could be directed to an algorithm?

Such a scenario could allow human psychiatrists to spend their time on more complex cases that benefit from their expertise. In 2025, the average psychiatry visit costs either the consumer or insurer between $75 and $200, depending on the reimbursement code, state, and available insurance coverage. Using current estimates for compute and energy, an algorithmic visit with a psychiatrist could be competitively priced at one-fifth or one-tenth the cost.

We are used to seeing medical residents on hospital floors, providing direct patient care under the supervision of an attending doctor. Under high automation, could algorithms play a similar role and alleviate the access and workforce shortage in healthcare?

My educated guess is that high automation will first focus on primary care, chronic condition management, or mental health, tackling the simplest of diagnoses. AI doctors will likely emerge first in incorporated telemedicine or virtual care, where the ability of human doctors to read cues, expressions, and touch is already constrained. They will integrate seamlessly with existing human clinical care and may escalate many of the cases presented to them to human doctors. 

Sensory Equivalence is a Hard Technical Problem

I intentionally oversimplified the Level 3: High Automation scenarios by assuming sensory equivalence. That’s the concept that a human doctor and an algorithm are dealing with the same input data, from different senses. But that’s actually a big assumption to make.

Let’s return to the analogy of self-driving cars. Lidar [light detection and ranging] was an essential breakthrough that allowed cars to perceive the constantly changing world around them, reading the movement of cars, pedestrians, buses, and bicyclists. It provides precise depth perception, detecting objects’ size, shape, and distance far more accurately than cameras or radar sensors alone. While there are alternative approaches, including Tesla’s camera-based system, Lidar has played a crucial role in the development of autonomous vehicles. Without depth perception, deep learning AI models couldn’t learn to drive.

We are not great at communication when we see a doctor. We often withhold relevant health information because we feel shame or stigma about admitting to our actions or behaviors. We dismiss what we believe are unrelated symptoms. Add to these cultural differences, language barriers, and concerns about insurance coverage, and it is no wonder communication in healthcare settings is so challenging.

And yet, doctors are skilled at building a complete picture with incomplete data to make a diagnosis. From the moment they see the patient, it’s an interactive process. Humans have a remarkable ability to merge raw sensory data from sight, sound, context, and intuition. 

Deep learning advances about a decade ago helped computers get remarkably better at face and image recognition, detecting microexpressions, gaze, and subtle body language. Current vision-language models are better at image segmentation and understanding depth perception, and are compatible with video. Similarly, haptic and tactile sensors are helping machines develop a bit more of the human sense of touch. Advancements in flexible electronic skins can detect pressure, temperature, texture, and vibrations. Perhaps at some point in the future medical robots, either at home or the doctor’s office, could achieve parity with human sensing ability. For the moment, though, there is still an inconceivable gap between human observational skills and the most advanced machine vision and perception technologies. 

Level 4: Complete Automation

Level 4: Complete Automation is the final stage of autonomous health. Here, machines don’t just make common diagnostic and treatment decisions, but all the decisions. Only a small set of human doctors and healthcare professionals would be required, and their principal responsibility would be to oversee, improve, and train the algorithms.

This iteration of machines doing most healthcare work seems impossible to imagine, and it may perhaps never manifest. But if our society does ever achieve complete automation of care, our descendants may romanticize human-based healthcare as a charming and quaint period in human history. Just as we think of artisans in the Middle Ages using wooden looms to make textiles, so might our descendants try to imagine humans measuring vitals and drawing blood. In this framework, Complete Automation requires AI to meet all the technical requirements of the high-automation state, and to do so consistently and in every complex situation. 

I’m used to being shocked by the rate of innovation. Nonetheless, I believe fully autonomous health, if it ever comes, is several decades away. Even if the underlying sensing and algorithmic decision-making abilities were impeccable compared to our human healthcare workforce, our society is not ready for it. It would take at least a generation of humanity, maybe more, to accept healthcare without human providers. 

How We Move Forward 

Computer scientists and technologists, including myself, tend to underestimate the clinical and social complexity of healthcare problems. There is a good reason for this human error. Historically, when a machine learning system excels at real-world problems, it often ends up solving the problem in a completely different way from the manual human process. The technical way a smartphone understands and summarizes human voice calls has little in common with human transcribers.

Healthcare is different. Deploying increasing autonomy in an existing healthcare economy is like replacing the jet turbine engine of the airplane with a portable nuclear reactor while it’s still airborne. It’s impossible to recreate an AI healthcare experience and economy in complete isolation from today’s human-centered healthcare experience. By definition, this is a hybrid transition. As I discuss in my new book, The Machines Will See You Now, emerging capabilities need to augment, empower and partner, not replace the role of human beings. 

Doctors, nurses, and other healthcare providers will play a pivotal role in accelerating the paradigm shift to high automation and complete automation. They will help create and train these models, and they will critically evaluate their accuracy and safety. Most doctors, nurses, and administrators I meet are accelerants of this change, but want to ensure these technologies are safe, tested and validated. 

The business of healthcare will look different too. How venture capitalists and private equity firms invest in hospital systems, large group practices, and innovative companies will continue to evolve. The market valuations and types of capital available are dramatically greater for AI and technology companies than they are for hospitals and medical practices, which today are lower-margin, lower-growth, service-oriented businesses.

Meanwhile, regulators, state, and federal agencies will need to find a balance between protecting consumers from risks and encouraging innovation. AI researchers and large tech companies could spend billions on LLMs fine-tuned for clinical diagnosis and treatment tasks, but without the requisite policy and regulatory changes, regulators could unintentionally handicap the potential impact on better care and lower costs. Or, in the quest for the best model, companies could lose sight of the importance of protecting consumer data and privacy. 

As we automate the lifesaving work of doctors and nurses and other practitioners, these are the kinds of questions we must be asking. Automation promises a world with less burden on providers and clinicians, where costs are reined in, and care is more personalized, more effective, and even delightful. But without a road map, and without being clear about what we expect from that transition, we could be writing ourselves into our own sci-fi dystopia.

item.title: More schools are banning cell phones. The academic benefits haven’t materialized
item.description:
School cell phone bans aren’t as new as you might think. While a growing number of states have adopted them over the past three years, the practice dates to 1989, when Maryland prohibited the devices (and pagers) in an attempt to limit in-school communication among students who may have been involved in illegal activities.

By 2009, in fact, nine out of 10 schools had banned cell phones. But that number began to drop as smartphones spread and parents wanted to be able to reach their kids in emergencies. Now that school phone bans are revving up again, questions are resurfacing about how effective they are at boosting test scores and reducing bullying.

The early data suggest the results haven’t been as positive as many expected.

A study from Stanford University’s Institute for Economic Policy Research and the National Bureau of Economic Research, released earlier this year, found virtually no impact on test scores in schools that have enforced bans for the past three years.

That surprised the researchers, all of whom are college professors, says Jason Baron, a co-author of the study and assistant professor of economics at Duke University.

“Our first reaction [when starting the study] was we might see a positive shift in test scores,” he tells Fast Company. “At a first glance, it makes perfect sense. We’re all educators. We have classrooms where we see students on their phones and it makes sense that if we ban their phones, they might pay more attention.”

On reflection, though, the lack of movement wasn’t so surprising. Test scores are difficult to move in general, and removing a phone doesn’t guarantee students will pay attention. They might doodle instead. They might daydream. They might stare longingly at the classmate who barely knows they exist.

That’s something parents and legislators may have overlooked, Baron says.

There’s also little evidence, the authors wrote, that restricting phone usage improved other parts of the school environment. Attendance rates didn’t noticeably change, including chronic absenteeism. Nor was there a statistically significant change in online bullying or classroom attention.

Baron cautions against focusing too heavily on the bullying findings, however. That information came from survey data from a small set of schools and wasn’t as comprehensive as the testing data the team had access to. Still, he conceded, simply taking phones out of the classroom would likely not be enough to end the problem.

“It is plausible that banning phones inside of school will not impact bullying, since students have phones outside of school,” he said.

Despite those findings, there are some potential upsides to school phone bans. The data so far covers just three years, meaning longer-term trends could still emerge. And surveys measuring student well-being found that while disciplinary infractions increased and reported well-being declined in the first year, by year three the number of incidents had returned to pre-ban levels and some students said their well-being had improved.

“If you’re someone that cares only about test results, then you might not be super impressed with these results,” says Baron. “It truly depends on what your goal is with banning phones.”

Baron says the team plans to continue studying schools that have enforced bans, with the next batch of data expected later this year.

While the impact of school phone bans has been negligible so far, support for them remains strong. A Pew Research Center survey in late July found that more than three-quarters of adults supported banning cellphones in classrooms for middle- and high-school students. And for the first time, a majority of adults supported banning the devices for the entire school day.

A growing number of states now have some form of cellphone ban. Just seven states currently have no limits on cell phone usage. More than 30 states ban phones in classrooms, while others impose more limited restrictions.

Prof Lyla Mehta says the glacial floods and loss of life are a stark reminder that climate disruption is global and highly unequal. Plus letters from Lynda McDonald and Jan Bengtsson

The recent glacial collapse and catastrophic floods in Nepal and Tibet are not isolated tragedies (Report, 28 August). They reflect accelerating climate disruption that disproportionately affects the countries and people that are least responsible for global emissions.

As climate change intensifies, glaciers around the world, including in the Himalayas, are melting at unprecedented rates, destabilising ecosystems and causing glacial collapse and ice-and-rock landslides, destroying settlements, villages and livelihoods in minutes. No one died when a Swiss glacier collapsed last year, owing to early-warning systems that were in place. But a lack of early-warning systems means that the disaster in Nepal and Tibet has led to hundreds of deaths and thousands missing.

item.title: The Guardian view on Nigeria’s kidnappings: a country can’t prosper when going to school is a danger | Editorial
item.description:
Abductions are resurging and may be spreading to new areas – with young children among the victims. A military response alone won’t work

Early last month, Nigeria’s government announced the largest single-day hostage rescue in its history, with the freeing of 300 people who had been taken in raids in two north central states. Celebrations were short-lived. Barely a fortnight later, gunmen abducted up to 600 worshippers from a mosque in Niger state. Nigerians paid kidnappers nearly $6m in ransoms in the year to June, according to a new report from the Lagos-based consultancy SBM Intelligence – more than triple the total in the previous 12-month period. More than 7,800 people were abducted, a two-thirds increase, and more than 1,100 killed, including almost 900 civilians.

When Boko Haram abducted almost 300 schoolgirls from their school in Chibok, Borno state in 2014, it made headlines worldwide. Yet around 45 children, mostly aged between two and five, remain missing after they were snatched from schools in Mussa, in north-eastern Borno state, in May. There is growing concern that kidnappings may be spreading to new areas. Forty-six students and staff were abducted from three schools in the south-western state of Oyo in the same month; they were rescued in July.

item.title: The Guardian view on press freedom: to defend democracy, stand up for journalists | Editorial
item.description:
The lack of justice for Daphne Caruana Galizia in Malta casts a shadow on reporters everywhere

The acquittal of Yorgen Fenech, who was on trial in Malta for involvement in the murder of the journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia, is a devastating blow for justice and press freedom. Nine years after her car was blown up, it seems increasingly unlikely that anyone will be held to account for ordering and paying for her death. Mr Fenech’s admissions that he knew about the murder before it happened, and gave money to the middle-man who paid the killers, make it hard to understand why he was found not guilty on the lesser charge of association.

All killings of journalists are wrong. The bomb placed in Caruana Galizia’s car was especially shocking, as such brazen violence is usually associated with war zones or states overrun by organised crime. The fact that this acquittal came two months after those of three men accused of murdering another journalist, Lyra McKee, in Northern Ireland, adds to a grim impression of impunity for killers. While McKee is not thought to have been targeted in the way that Caruana Galizia was, the inability of police and prosecutors to secure convictions in either case points to wider problems.

item.title: When does rage help us, and when does it harm us? Ukraine has taught me the answers | Charlotte Higgins
item.description:
Fury at Russia’s death and destruction has fuelled art, action and resistance. But eventually, rage’s fire is all-consuming

Twice, I have heard Ukrainians perform Verdi’s Requiem. Once in Lviv, last Maundy Thursday, and once last month, under the great dome of St Paul’s Cathedral in London. In St Paul’s, performed by the Ukrainian Freedom Orchestra with the Philharmonia Chorus, the great Dies irae – “day of anger” – unfurled in an operatic gale of fury, reverberating so powerfully around Wren’s lofty spaces that the music felt like thunder echoing between mountain peaks.

In Lviv, where it was performed by a Ukrainian chorus and orchestra, the evening began with a call to remember the war dead. Lviv’s lay a mile up the road: 153 graves when I first visited in autumn 2022, and by this year more than 1,000. Ranks and ranks of soldiers killed in their 20s, 30s and 40s, each grave planted with flowers and plants, flags flying above. On that occasion, Dies irae – in the more sober acoustic of the Lviv Philharmonic Hall – seemed to contain the furious ache of grief. Certainly I have never heard a more wrathful day of anger.

item.title: Britain’s schools are failing its young people – and 1m Neets are paying the price | Simon Jenkins
item.description:
Obsessed with exams, devoid of vocational training: there is a total mismatch between schools and life beyond their gates

Blame the schools. Alan Milburn’s report on Neets, published in May, was one of the most damning comments on the welfare state I have read. It described a new generation of a million mostly poor Britons now encouraged to fare worse, not better, than their parents. This means, said Milburn, that “the great British promise” – the advance of generations – is being broken. A sizeable chunk of the population is going backwards.

The number of young people not in education, employment or training – one in eight of all 16- to 24-year-olds – is rising fast and will be 1.25 million by 2030. More than 80% of them claim to want to find a job, education or training. A third even have “good GCSEs”, but 44% of them are on state benefits, now costing £8.1bn. Many of them suffer from anxiety and other disabilities, according to the NHS. The number of young people with special educational needs has doubled in 10 years. Mental ill-health is bordering on pandemic levels.

item.title: The world is being driven to the brink by thugs and dictators, but there is a route to a brighter future | Simon Tisdall
item.description:
It’s no surprise some analysts say we are already in the midst of the third world war, but ordinary people have more power than we think

Don’t look up! The world is a mess. The sky could fall in any day. Unending wars, expanding humanitarian crises, rising authoritarianism, dysfunctional democracies, rampant racial and religious extremism, and unchecked lawlessness cast a dark cloud as the west’s new political year begins. Set all that against a backdrop of staggering global economic inequality, corporate and individual greed, irresponsible government indebtedness, dangerous AI gambles, climate breakdown and proliferating nuclear weapons, and a truly apocalyptic global outlook begins to take shape. It’s enough to make anyone shut their eyes, cover their ears and utter a Munch-like scream. And it’s only getting worse.

Democratic leaders who promise a better, safer, more optimistic future – what Britain’s freshly arrived prime minister, Andy Burnham, calls a “new era of possibility” – cannot escape this wider international context. Last week’s global bond market upheaval, sparked by external factors, left Burnham’s cash-strapped government struggling with sharply increased borrowing costs before he barely got started. The fact he chose Ukraine for his first overseas trip, while symbolically important, highlighted another grim reality. As a lead opponent of Vladimir Putin’s invasion, Britain now finds itself in a de facto state of war with Russia – and facing attack. Argentina, too, is eyeing UK defence vulnerabilities. These are not the sort of possibilities Burnham envisaged.

item.title: That sound you hear is not the world ending – it’s liberalism being monstered | Waleed Aly
item.description:
It turns out most of us no longer believe in progress. And when that happens, it quickly becomes a crisis for societies like ours

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Depending on your politics, the monsters are everywhere. Perhaps you see them in the form of tech billionaires and the artificial intelligence they’re developing. Perhaps you see them in the bin fire of social media they bequeathed us before that, or the legacy media that refuse to tell you “the truth”. You might see them in the manosphere, or the institutions teaching our kids gender fluidity. Maybe you see them in the migrant youth wielding machetes in the suburbs, or the refugee attempting to behead someone on a Belfast street. Or perhaps you see them in the violent anti-immigrant mobs that torched houses in response. If so, you’ll likely see them in the Marches for Australia or to Unite the Kingdom rallies, organised by far-right groups but attended by many more besides. You’ll almost certainly see them in at least one of Hamas, Israel or those local advocates at each other’s throats over the Middle East. I suspect you’ll see them in Russia but that can no longer be assumed. And I’d guess that you’d see them in at least one political party with a significant share of the vote.

Something in that paragraph probably outraged you. In which case, you’re probably seeing monsters in whoever sees different monsters from you. It would be easy here to make a point about polarisation. But I want to look at the deep disquiet that lies underneath.

It was a busy weekend for the insurgent and hard right, as Reform party delegates redoubled their commitment to women’s safety by physically attacking a female protester and Patriot Platform, a new group established by Danny Tommo, real name Daniel Thomas, arrived in Dover on Saturday, then Portsmouth on Sunday, dressed in balaclavas. No arrests were made in Dover, and therefore the protest was deemed peaceful. “A message was sent!” Thomas exclaimed later on his socials. “Now imagine how powerful the next message will be.” The next powerful message of peace the following day spurred the issuance of a dispersal order from Hampshire police, alongside some smashed windscreens (of police cars) and advice for local people to avoid the area.

The “stop the boats” narrative, along with a lot of Reform’s anti-immigrant rhetoric, has become increasingly bound up with a concern for the safety of women and children. It might be a slyly vague sentiment from Robert Jenrick, in which he doesn’t want his daughters sharing a neighbourhood with men “who broke into the country illegally, about whom we know next to nothing”, or it might be Zia Yusuf’s much more explicit complaint that the nation is prepared to “sacrifice British women and girls on the altar of diversity”. Protesters outside hotels housing asylum seekers get all their righteous wrath from the danger posed to women from foreign nationals, and Thomson stated his aims straightforwardly on Instagram – posting video of Saturday’s protest, he wrote: “Protect our country! And more importantly our women and children! This is our warning!”

item.title: The Guardian view on the far right’s real weapon: it is the politics of powerlessness | Editorial
item.description:
From Dover to Saxony-Anhalt, extremists thrive when voters believe established parties can no longer deliver security, prosperity or meaningful change

What links the thuggish masked agitation in southern England this weekend and the far-right Alternative für Deutschland’s (AfD) best-ever result in a German state – where it more than doubled the 21% vote it received five years ago? Several hundred men in balaclavas blocking an A road are not the same as a party winning a landslide election. But both events draw on the idea that the political system has lost control. The extremists in Dover and Portsmouth dramatise this claim; the electoral result in Germany threatens to institutionalise it.

The prospect of Germany’s first far-right-led state government since the second world war carries real consequences. In Saxony-Anhalt it could see power handed to a party hostile to migrants, Islam, LGBTQ+ rights and climate policy. Alarmingly, it has senior figures linked to former neo-Nazi groups. About 170,000 foreign nationals live among 2 million people in Saxony-Anhalt – and roughly a fifth of the state’s doctors were born abroad. The grim paradox is that an AfD government could oversee the very state intelligence service that has classified the party as “rightwing extremist”.

item.title: ‘This is dangerous’: slime moulds and the bitter debate over the nature of intelligence
item.description:
Scientists are battling over whether supposedly simple organisms should be considered ‘intelligent’. The outcome could reshape our understanding of the natural world – and our own place within it

Forty years ago, as an undergraduate in Hokkaido, Toshiyuki Nakagaki came upon a lemon-yellow stain in a petri dish. That encounter turned him into a doyen of slime mould research – and fed a storm of biological and philosophical debate about the meanings of life and intelligence that persists to this day. Before, no one would have called a slime mould “intelligent”; the popular adjective, in fact, was “simple”. “A simple mass of protoplasm,” one 1895 description ran; “among the most simple of organisms”, said another. And it was hard to argue otherwise. A slime mould can appear to be just a small cell, capable only of feeding and reproducing. Simple is as simple does.

Of that first meeting, Nakagaki said: “I was just impressed with how fast it moved.” Physarum polycephalum, the slime mould species in that petri dish, has a top speed of 1cm an hour. For amoebic organisms, that’s gold-medal standard. At first glance, Physarum seems to spread as irregularly as ink on blotting paper, but in fact it senses its meals of bacteria or other microbes and reaches for them with a long, thin finger of protoplasm – which not only digests its food but then forages further or pulls back into the rest of the mould. It’s impossible to watch a slime mould over many days without sensing some deliberation at play.

item.title: How ‘Star Trek’ helped invent the future
item.description:
Star Trek first beamed into our lives at 8:30 p.m. on Sept. 8, 1966, and the science fiction world was never the same. The show, though canceled after just three seasons, went on to become a lasting pop culture phenomenon that has spawned an entertainment empire, with movies, spinoffs, merchandise, and a fan following that few intellectual properties can match.

But Star Trek proved to be more than just an entertainment property. The technology the show imagined inspired many future developers to try to recreate the gadgets they saw growing up. And some of those fantastical devices have become part of daily life, even if we’re still a long way from launching our own five-year mission to explore strange new worlds.

Here’s some of the on-screen technology that has become real.

Communicators

Captain Kirk and crew stayed in touch with each other and the Enterprise via a handheld device that flipped open. Modern technology managed to replicate that by 1989, with the release of the first Motorola StarTAC phone, and arguably perfected it with the Razr in 2004.

The technology, of course, has continued to improve, and the “communicators” we carry today, in the form of iPhones and the wide assortment of Android devices, do a lot more than just let us talk to others. Still, Martin Cooper, who has been credited with the invention of the first handheld cellular phone in the 1970s, said his inspiration for the first cell phone was, in fact, Star Trek‘s communicator.

Universal translators

Lt. Uhura had lots of duties on board the Enterprise, but figuring out what the aliens were saying wasn’t always one of them. That was the job of the ship’s universal translator. Today, there are several tools that provide instant translation of foreign languages, though they’re not too useful should a Gorn want to strike up a conversation.

Those range from apps such as Google Translate and iTranslate to AI-assisted earbuds like the Samsung Galaxy Buds4 line and Timekettle’s W4 Pro, as well as handheld translators like the Vasco V4 Language Translator Device.

Voice-interface computers

In 1966, seeing Mr. Spock talk with the ship’s computer was something few people could imagine. Today, millions of people do that on a regular basis, interacting with the Amazon Echo device sitting on their counter, asking Siri to call up some information, or even telling their vacuum to tidy up the floors. Most states, in fact, require drivers to avoid picking up their cell phones while behind the wheel but are just fine with voice interactions.

Medical tricorders

Dr. McCoy isn’t the only person with a tricorder medical scanner, though his is still much better than anything we have at the moment. A decade ago, a company called Scanadu showed off a handheld device that measured five vital signs in roughly 30 seconds. That company was acquired six years ago by Israeli healthcare startup Healthy.io.

Today’s smartwatches, meanwhile, fill some of the same roles as a tricorder, monitoring your heart rate, sleep schedule, blood pressure, and more.

Replicators

The advent of 3D printers has given us the ability to summon devices from thin air, much like viewers have seen in subsequent Star Trek shows (though it sometimes takes a day or two for them to assemble). The technology can create everything from custom prosthetics to engine parts to rocket engines, as used on the Aeon 1 rocket in 2023.

3D-printed food as it was presented on the show isn’t possible, but specialized devices can create edible layers using food powders and a liquid binder. That can make a decent confection, but it’s still a long way from learning to make Gagh.

Hyposprays

Shots on Star Trek were needle-free, something any child watching was particularly envious of. What few realized, though, was that jet injectors were actually already a thing at the time. The device uses high-pressure gas to propel a high-velocity stream of liquid medication through the skin. The tech is still around today, but doctors haven’t given up the needle for the most part. Sorry, kids.

(Coming soon?) Warp drive

OK, no, the warp drive is still a fantasy. Faster-than-light travel, as NASA will tell anyone who asks, is still imaginary at present. That doesn’t mean it has given up on the idea. NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio, houses the Breakthrough Propulsion Physics Project, where NASA engineers are hoping to produce “near-term, credible, and measurable progress toward the technology breakthroughs needed to revolutionize space travel and enable interstellar voyages.” The Tau Zero Foundation, meanwhile, is also seeking advances in propulsion that could make interstellar flight possible.
